African rice (Oryza glaberrima) is a species of its own, distinct from Asian rice. According to the source, it was first domesticated and grown about 3,000 years ago in the inland delta of the Niger, in present-day Mali. From there its cultivation spread across West Africa.

At Nkang in central Cameroon, archaeologists have examined pits from a settlement at least 2,700 years old. In one of the pits, which radiocarbon dating shows was used about 2,400–2,500 years ago, banana phytoliths were stuck to pieces of pottery. Phytoliths are microscopic silica particles that form in plants. Bananas have no wild ancestors in Africa, so they must have been brought there.

text.en: Wikipedia’s article on Nkang describes the finds as the first evidence of bananas in Africa. The article on bananas says the phytoliths are confirmed as banana, but that the early date is uncertain: only 25 phytoliths were found, and layers may have been mixed. According to that article, all other banana finds in Africa date from the first millennium AD or later.

summary.en: The Luxmanda settlement in northern Tanzania was discovered in 2012. Radiocarbon dating shows it was occupied about 3,200–2,900 years ago. It is the largest and southernmost known settlement of the early East African herding culture called the Savanna Pastoral Neolithic. Its people relied heavily on their animals: cattle, sheep, goats and donkeys. Residues in the pottery show that they mostly cooked meat and, to a lesser extent, milk. The genome of an infant girl who died about 3,100 years ago shows that about 38 per cent of her ancestry was linked to early farmers in the Levant.

A foot bone from the site of Spoegrivier in Namaqualand, South Africa, has been radiocarbon dated to 2105 ± 65 years before present. After calibration, its age most likely lies between about 200 BC and AD 110. An analysis of the bone’s proteins, published in 2021, confirmed that it comes from a sheep. According to the study, it is the earliest directly dated evidence of domestic animals in southern Africa.

text.en: Teeth from Leopard Cave in Namibia, from just over 2,000 years ago, were interpreted in 2012 as sheep or goat. A 2020 study showed that they come from wild springbok, and the 2021 study on Spoegrivier does not challenge that identification. The point is the village of Spoegrivier according to Wikidata; the exact position of the site is not given in the source.

summary.en: Deriba is a caldera, a large cauldron-shaped depression, in the Jebel Marra massif in Darfur, western Sudan. About 3,500 years ago, 3520 ± 100 years before present, the volcano had a large explosive eruption of the Plinian type, rated 4 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index. Activity then continued with a cone inside the caldera and side vents, possibly into historical times. The caldera measures about 4.8 × 6.4 kilometres, and its rim is the highest point in Sudan. There are hot springs and fumaroles, and the volcano is now regarded as dormant, not extinct.

The Mare aux Songes swamp on Mauritius holds the bones of more than 300 dodos and many other animals. The bones were deposited over a few centuries about 4,000 years ago. According to researchers, the island was hit by a severe and prolonged drought about 4,200 years ago. The animals went to the water in the swamp, got stuck in the mud and died. In the 2005 excavation, almost two thirds of the bones came from giant tortoises of the genus Cylindraspis.

The Piton de la Fournaise volcano on Réunion has collapsed several times. The Enclos Fouqué caldera formed through collapses in three episodes, about 250,000, 65,000 and 5,000 years ago. An explosive eruption about 4,700 years ago may have reached 5 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index. The last major collapse of the volcano’s flank is believed to have happened about 4,500 years ago.

According to the source, the Kintampo culture was founded by farmers and herders from the Sahara between about 2500 and 1400 BC. Archaeologists have studied at least three dozen sites in savanna, wooded savanna and rainforest in present-day Ghana. The people grew pearl millet, cowpeas, yams and oil palm among other plants, kept goats, sheep and cattle, and hunted wild animals.

text.en: In one place the source says the culture was founded between 2500 and 1400 BC, and in another that the Kintampo tradition appeared 3,600–3,200 years ago, that is about 1650–1250 BC. The span here follows the first statement. According to the source, the rock shelters had been abandoned by the second century BC.

summary.en: The Urewe culture was an early Iron Age culture around Lake Victoria. Its earliest dated artefacts come from the Kagera Region of Tanzania, and its sites date from the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD. The culture reached Kivu in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, western Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, and was most widespread in the first six centuries AD.

text.en: The source dates the sites from the 5th century BC, but also says that the culture emerged around the turn of the second to the first millennium BC, that is about 1000 BC. The span here follows the dated sites. The article is flagged as needing more citations, and the point is the archaeological site of Urewe in Kenya according to Wikidata.

summary.en: Around Akjoujt in western Mauritania, copper was mined and smelted long before the Common Era. Traces of mining continue until about 300 BC, and radiocarbon dates from the Grotte aux Chauves-souris mine show that the copper ore malachite was mined and smelted there in the early 5th century BC. How the technique arrived is disputed. It has been linked to the spread of Berbers into the western Sahara and the Sahel, and the researcher Michael Bisson has pointed to ties with the Early Bronze Age of Western Europe and Phoenician North Africa.

text.en: Wikipedia’s article on Akjoujt says copper was mined and smelted there as early as about 1000 BC. The article on copper metallurgy in Africa dates the beginning to about 850 BC and the mining to about 850–300 BC, but says elsewhere that copper metallurgy in the Akjoujt region has been dated to the second and early first millennium BC. The span here starts at the figure of about 1000 BC.

summary.en: King Arnekhamani of Kush, who according to the source reigned about 220–215 BC, had the Lion Temple built at Musawwarat es-Sufra in present-day Sudan. The temple is dedicated to the god Apedemak, who is shown with three heads in the reliefs on its outer walls. Its largest structure is the Great Enclosure, a labyrinth-like complex of about 45,000 square metres, much of which was built in the 3rd century BC.

The Medracen is a large round tumulus of dressed stone in the countryside about 90 kilometres south of Constantine in Algeria. It is regarded as a royal mausoleum built by the Berber kingdom of Numidia. Around its base stand sixty Doric columns, partly built into the wall, beneath a cornice in Egyptian style, and its upper part rises in steps reminiscent of the pyramids of Egypt.

text.en: Some sources date the Medracen to the 4th century BC. Others link the monument to King Masinissa, who reigned 202–148 BC, and date it to the end of the 3rd century or the first half of the 2nd century BC. The span here covers both datings.

summary.en: Senegal and the Gambia have more than 1,000 stone circles and burial mounds. The generally accepted range for them runs from the 3rd century BC to the 16th century AD. The monuments mark graves, and at Sine Ngayène the burials seem to have come first and the stones to have been raised later. There is no agreement on who built them; the Serer themselves attribute the monuments to a people they call the Soos.

text.en: The sites for which the source gives dates are younger than the start of the range: the burial mounds at Wassu AD 927–1305, Wanar 7th–15th centuries AD and Sine Ngayène about AD 700–1350. The start in the 3rd century BC is the beginning of the range the source calls generally accepted.

caption.en: Modern photo (2006) of the Wassu stone circles in the Gambia, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: At Katanda on the Semliki River in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, archaeologists have found several barbed harpoon heads made of bone. According to Wikipedia they are about 90,000 years old. The site also holds many catfish bones, and the size of the harpoons suits catching fully grown catfish. A 2018 article counts them among the oldest known specialised bone tools south of the Sahara.

text.en: When the first harpoon head was dated, some archaeologists doubted the age, because the tool seemed too advanced for its time. According to Wikipedia, more harpoons of the same kind have been found since and the dates have been confirmed. The 2018 article (Bouzouggar et al.) gives the same age, about 90,000 years, but refers to the same 1995 study and is therefore not an independent second source. The point on the map is the start of the Semliki River near Ishango, not the find site itself, which the sources do not give more precisely.

summary.en: In the Dar es-Soltan 1 cave on Morocco’s Atlantic coast, about 10 kilometres south-west of Rabat, researchers have found a tool made from a rib, probably from an animal of the bovid family. They interpret it as a knife that could be used for several tasks. The layer where the tool lay has been dated by luminescence to about 90,000 years ago. According to the researchers, it is the oldest specialised bone tool in a well-dated setting that clearly belongs to the Aterian culture of North Africa.

text.en: The information comes from the researchers’ own 2018 article (Bouzouggar et al.). No second source has been compared. The age, about 90,400 ± 3,400 years, is a model built on several luminescence dates of the layer, not a date of the bone itself.

summary.en: Uan Muhuggiag is a rock shelter in the Tadrart Acacus mountains in south-western Libya, in the middle of the Sahara. There archaeologists found the remains of a boy of about two and a half who had been embalmed. His organs had been removed, and the body lay in a foetal position in a sack of antelope skin with a layer of leaves. Around his neck he wore a necklace of ostrich eggshell. According to Wikipedia the site was in use from no later than the sixth millennium BC until about 2700 BC, and it also has rock paintings, bones of domestic cattle and pottery. The mummy is now in the Red Castle Museum in Tripoli.

text.en: Wikipedia gives several dates that do not fit together. The skin the mummy was wrapped in has been dated to 5405 ± 180 years BP, which the article says corresponds to about 6250 calendar years before present. Elsewhere it says the mummy is about 5,600 years old, and a date obtained via the deepest charcoal layer where the mummy was found gives an older age, 7438 ± 220 years BP. The span here, about 4300–3650 BC, follows the calibrated age of the skin and the age of 5,600 years.

summary.en: Tassili n'Ajjer is a plateau in south-eastern Algeria, near the borders with Libya and Niger. It holds a great number of rock engravings and rock paintings, and the area has been a World Heritage Site since 1982. The oldest images are presumed to be about 12,000 years old and show wild animals and hunting. Later came the so-called Round Head figures, people with round heads who seem to float, and later still images of domestic cattle, horses and camels.

text.en: According to Wikipedia the sources vary considerably, and how the art should be dated is debated. The age of 12,000 years for the oldest images is a presumption. According to luminescence dates of nearby sediments, most works are from 10,000–8,000 years ago or later, and the chronology changes as new research appears. The year shown here is therefore very approximate.

caption.en: Modern photo (2023) of a rock painting with human and animal figures at Tanzoumaitak in Tassili n’Ajjer near Djanet in Algeria, not from the time of the event. Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Enkapune Ya Muto, also called Twilight Cave, is a rock shelter on the Mau Escarpment above the Naivasha basin in Kenya’s part of the Rift Valley. In one of the layers archaeologists have found 13 complete perforated ostrich eggshell beads, 12 unfinished beads and almost 600 shell fragments. This suggests that beads were made on the spot. The beads have been dated to about 40,000 years ago.

text.en: Wikipedia gives different figures for the beads: the introduction says 40,000 years, the text 39,900 years BP and the table 37,000 years BP for the same layer. The article also says that some dates from the site are less reliable, because the samples were small or had been contaminated during long storage. The year shown here is therefore approximate.

summary.en: The Naqada culture is Egypt’s culture in the period before the pharaohs, named after the town of Naqada in Upper Egypt. It is divided into three phases, Naqada I–III, from about 4000 BC to shortly before 3000 BC. Among other things people made black-topped pottery and painted vessels, and early on they had contacts with Nubia, the oases of the Western Desert and the eastern Mediterranean. Obsidian came all the way from Ethiopia. Over time grave goods became richer and the differences between an elite and ordinary people clearer. The last phase coincides with the time of the first pharaohs.

text.en: Wikipedia’s introduction gives about 4000–3000 BC. Werner Kaiser’s 1957 chronology began around 4000 BC, and in its modern version the last phase, Naqada III, falls at about 3300–2900 BC. A 2013 radiocarbon study instead gives a start between 3800 and 3700 BC and an end around 3100 BC. The place on the map is the town of Naqada, but the culture spread over large parts of Egypt.

summary.en: About 25,600 years ago Taupō Volcano on the North Island of New Zealand had a gigantic eruption, the Oruanui eruption. It is counted as the most recent known supereruption on Earth. The eruption lasted only a few months but threw out more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of ash and rock. Ash fell over the whole North Island and the northern part of the South Island, and it has been found in the ice of Antarctica, about 5,000 kilometres away. Where the ground collapsed, part of Lake Taupō lies today.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 25,675 ± 90 years before present, after a correction with the IntCal20 calibration curve. The 2017 study by Dunbar et al. recalculates the age of the eruption as 25,580 ± 258 years before present. The ash layer in the WDC06A ice core from West Antarctica is dated there to about 25,318 years before 1950, which agrees with the eruption age within the margin of error. The span here covers both ages for the eruption. Older works give 26,500 years, and according to Wikipedia the age may be corrected again.

caption.en: Modern photo (2012) of ash aggregates in ignimbrite from the Oruanui eruption of Taupō volcano, New Zealand, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: At the dry lake of Lake Mungo in New South Wales, the geologist Jim Bowler found in 1968 the burnt bones of a woman, now known as Mungo Lady. According to Wikipedia this is one of the oldest known cremations in the world, and it suggests that people already then had complex burial rituals. According to a 2003 study she is about 40,000 years old. Her remains were returned to the Aboriginal groups in 1992 and reburied in 2022, together with Mungo Man.

text.en: The Wikipedia page Lake Mungo remains states that Mungo Lady (LM1) has been radiocarbon dated to 24,700–19,030 years ago. According to the page Lake Mungo, Bowler’s 2003 luminescence (OSL) study changed the age of both Mungo Lady and Mungo Man to about 40,000 years, and the page Lake Mungo remains says the study found the two to be roughly the same age. The point on the map is the lake, not the find site itself.

caption.en: Modern satellite photo (2024) of the dry lakebed at Lake Mungo and the dune along its eastern edge, not from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The northern common cuscus is a marsupial from New Guinea that also lives on several islands further away. According to Wikipedia it was introduced to the island of New Ireland in the Bismarck Archipelago between 10,000 and 20,000 years ago, and to the Solomon Islands only less than 6,000 years ago. A 2022 research review describes how the cuscus was moved between islands about 20,000 years ago, probably for its meat.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the cuscus was introduced to New Ireland between 10,000 and 20,000 years ago, but does not say who brought it there. The 2022 review by Roberts et al. mentions that the cuscus was moved between islands about 20,000 years ago, probably for its meat, but does not mention New Ireland. The span here follows Wikipedia. The point on the map is the centre of the island.

summary.en: Lake Bonneville was a large lake in North America during the Ice Age, about 83,000 square kilometres. About 17,400 years ago the water rose so high that it broke through a natural dam at Red Rock Pass in present-day Idaho. The flood rushed through the Snake River valley, carved a deep canyon and waterfalls such as Shoshone Falls, and reached the Pacific Ocean via the Columbia River. Unlike the Missoula floods, it happened only once.

text.en: Wikipedia gives two figures: about 14,500 years by radiocarbon and about 17,400 calendar years after calibration. This is the same date expressed in two ways, and the year here follows the calendar years. The article on Red Rock Pass mentions only the figure 14,500 years.

summary.en: By the Great Lakes of North America, people in the Archaic period worked native copper, which was found in veins and nuggets near Lake Superior, for example on Isle Royale and the Keweenaw Peninsula. According to Wikipedia the culture lasted from about 6500 to 1000 BC, and towards the end copper was used mostly for ornaments and status items. The researchers behind a 2022 study describe it as the earliest known use of native copper for tools in the world.

text.en: The sources give different starts and ends. Wikipedia says about 6500–1000 BC, but its introduction also gives 6500–1580 BC for some sites. The article mentions new radiocarbon dates from 2021 that make the oldest known copper object at least about 8,500 years old. The 2022 study (Bebber et al.) calculates that the tradition began 7,520–6,180 years ago, but that copper may have been used as early as about 9,000 years ago. The study places the end of the tradition 4,840–4,190 years ago and says that intensive copper mining had largely ceased by about 3,300 years ago.

summary.en: Windover is a small pond near Titusville in Florida where people buried their dead in the peat about 8,000–7,000 years ago. Archaeologists have found about 168 individuals, and at least 90 of them had preserved brain tissue. One of the dead was a boy aged 14–16 with open spina bifida, who was probably paralysed from the waist down. That he still lived so long suggests, according to Wikipedia, that the group cared for him for about 15 years.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the burials to about 8,000–7,000 years before present and elsewhere to 7,000–8,000 years ago. Two bones have been radiocarbon dated to 7,210 and 7,320 years BP. The number of individuals is given differently in the article: 168, 169 or 177.

summary.en: Huaca Prieta is a large mound on the Pacific coast in the Chicama Valley in northern Peru. People have been there since about 14,500 years ago, long before pottery existed in the area. In the mound researchers have found cotton fabrics about 6,000 years old, and some of them are dyed blue with indigo. According to Wikipedia this is the earliest known use of indigo as a dye, about 1,500 years before indigo was used in Egypt under the Fifth Dynasty.

text.en: Wikipedia says in the text that the fabrics are about 6,000 years old, but the caption of a fabric fragment in the same article gives about 2500 BC. The year here follows the text. The age of the earliest presence also varies slightly in the article, 14,500 or 15,000 years.

summary.en: In the desert of the Tarim Basin, people who were buried about 4,000 years ago have been preserved as mummies. When researchers studied the genomes of 13 of the early mummies in 2021, they found a local population that had long lived in isolation. This speaks against older theories that they descended from migrant groups such as the Afanasievo culture. Milk proteins in their dental calculus nevertheless suggest that they kept livestock.

text.en: The span here follows the 13 individuals in the 2021 study, which the article on the Tarim mummies dates to 2135–1623 BC; the article on Xiaohe gives about 2100–1700 BC for the same study. The oldest mummies, at Qäwrighul, are dated in one part of the article to about 2135–1939 BC and in another to about 1800 BC. The oldest graves at Xiaohe are dated to about 1884–1736 BC.

summary.en: In the ruin mound of Tell Leilan, the ancient city of Shekhna in north-eastern Syria, there is a layer of soil just under a metre thick with no trace of people at all. Researchers have linked it to a severe drought that began around 2200 BC and hit farming. It is part of the 4.2-kiloyear event, a climate shift with traces also in the Indus Valley and China. Around 2170 BC large parts of the northern plains were abandoned, and many people fled south, which may have weakened the Akkadian Empire.

text.en: The article on Tell Leilan describes a drought lasting three centuries, while the article on the 4.2-kiloyear event says the event most likely lasted the whole 22nd century BC. Some researchers argue that it was not a global drought with a clear timeline, and the claim that the drought brought down the Akkadian Empire is presented as a claim, not as established.

summary.en: In the same year as the Battle of Actium, the seventh year of Herod the Great as king, an earthquake shook Judea. The historian Josephus relates that cattle and people were killed by collapsing buildings, while Herod’s army escaped because it was camped in the open. In the ruins at Qumran there is a crack through a ritual bath and collapsed rooms that may be the work of the quake, but the damage may also come from later attacks. Because archaeologists have found little destruction, the magnitude is estimated at only 6–6.5.

text.en: Josephus gives different death tolls in his two works: about 10,000 dead in the Antiquities of the Jews and 30,000 in The Jewish War. According to Wikipedia, the fact that Octavian’s march through Judea the following year mentions no devastation suggests that the quake was not a major catastrophe.

summary.en: The Persian king Darius I sent some trusted men to sail down the Indus. Among them was Scylax, a Greek whose home was Caryanda. Herodotus relates that they followed the river out to the sea, kept westward and after 30 months reached the place where an Egyptian king had once let Phoenicians set off to sail around Libya. Many historians think the purpose was to scout ahead of a conquest, not to explore.

text.en: The voyage is known only through Herodotus, who gives no year. Wikipedia says that Scylax was active in the 510s BC, and Darius I reigned 522–486 BC. Herodotus writes that the river flowed east, but the Indus flows south-west, and so some scholars doubt that the voyage took place at all.

summary.en: When Alexander the Great turned homeward from India in 326 BC, he had a fleet built on the Hydaspes river. Under the command of Nearchus it sailed down the Indus and then west along the coast, while Alexander himself marched through the desert of Gedrosia. The fleet then passed a hilly island that Nearchus called Morontobara, later identified with Manora at Karachi, made its way through the Strait of Hormuz and reached the mouth of the Tigris in 324 BC.

Around 2300 BC King Ur-Nanshe of Lagash received timber that ships from Dilmun had brought him. Dilmun lay on the Persian Gulf and passed goods between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. The capital was probably the mound of Qal'at al-Bahrain in northern Bahrain, where people lived from about 2300 BC. Most finds point to Bahrain, but some scholars have looked for Dilmun elsewhere on the Gulf.

The Sabaean kings in present-day Yemen built great irrigation works, among them the dam at Marib. The oldest inscription about it is from the time of King Yatha' Amar Watar I, 760–740 BC. According to Wikipedia the dam supported a flourishing culture for more than a thousand years. It broke several times and was repaired, but after water overtopped it in 570 or 575 it was abandoned.

text.en: Archaeological finds suggest that earth dams and canals existed at Marib as early as about 1750 BC, but that dating is described as tentative. Wikipedia calls the 8th century BC the most reliable dating of the Great Dam.

summary.en: Tomb number three at Mawangdui in Changsha was sealed in 168 BC. A man in his thirties lay there, and 28 books written on silk were placed with him. Among them were two medical works that no one had known before: one with prescriptions for 52 ailments and one on eleven channels in the body, and both describe treatment with moxibustion. Since acupuncture is absent from the texts, moxibustion may have been a primary treatment at the time.

In 1966 a Harvard student tripped over a tree root in the village of Ban Chiang in north-eastern Thailand and fell among old clay pots sticking up out of the path. Later excavations found crucibles and other signs that the villagers cast bronze themselves. The red-painted pots that made the site famous are, by contrast, much younger, from about 300 BC–AD 200.

text.en: When bronze casting began is still disputed. New radiocarbon analyses indicate that metalworking probably began around 2000–1700 BC, while Charles Higham’s analysis of bones gives a first settlement around 1500 BC and the start of the Bronze Age around 1000 BC. The first datings, which made Ban Chiang the site of the world’s oldest bronze casting, are today considered unlikely.

summary.en: Bronze frogs often sit on top of the great drums for which the Đông Sơn culture of northern Vietnam is best known. The metal top of the drum has a sun at its centre, and around it run rings depicting warships and warriors adorned with feathers. The culture is dated to about 1000 BC–AD 100; Vietnamese historians place its end at 1 BC.

The Korean Peninsula has more than 35,000 dolmens, about 40 per cent of all those in the world according to Wikipedia. The tombs are built of large stones with a heavy capstone, and they are linked to a ruling elite who also held rites at them. The custom of raising dolmens existed in Korea from the 7th century BC, among other places in Gochang in the south-west of the country, and died out around the 3rd century BC.

A copy of the Golden Man stands today at the top of the Independence Monument in Almaty, as a national symbol of Kazakhstan. The original was found in 1969 in a six-metre-high burial mound of the Saka, a Scythian people, near Issyk. The mound’s main grave had been robbed, but a side grave of spruce logs was untouched. In it lay a young person aged 16–18 in a costume with about 4,000 gold objects. Whether the person was a man or a woman cannot be determined.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the grave differently in different parts of the article. The introduction gives the 4th or 3rd century BC, the silver bowl is dated in one section to the 6th–5th century BC and in another to about the 4th century BC, and the gold objects in the captions to the 5th–4th century BC. The span here follows the introduction. The number of gold objects and the age of the dead person are also given slightly differently.

summary.en: The whole of Pāṇini’s grammar can be recited in about two hours, even though it contains nearly 4,000 short rules. The work is called the Aṣṭādhyāyī, is divided into eight chapters and is the earliest surviving grammar of Sanskrit. The rules describe how correct words and forms are built, and the work is usually taken to mark the beginning of Classical Sanskrit. Modern scholars have compared the system with formal models of language, and Frits Staal called Pāṇini the Indian Euclid. According to later inscriptions Pāṇini came from Salatura in Gandhara, probably in present-day northern Pakistan.

text.en: Scholars disagree about when Pāṇini lived. Several place him in the 6th or 5th century BC, others around 350 BC, and Wikipedia writes that most date him somewhere between the 6th–5th and the 4th century BC. The number of rules is given as 3,959 in one place in the article and 3,996 in another.

summary.en: In Gonabad in Iran, water has been led underground for about 2,700 years. The system is a qanat: a gently sloping tunnel that takes groundwater from an aquifer and lets it flow out to the fields by gravity, without pumps. Where the technique was born is not entirely clear: Iran, early in the first millennium BC, is usually named, but there are also sources that favour south-eastern Arabia.

Nine days on horseback or ninety on foot: that was how long the journey took on the Royal Road between Susa and Sardis, about 2,700 kilometres. The Persian Empire rebuilt and improved the road in the 5th century BC, probably under Darius I. Along it were 111 stations with fresh horses, so that the king’s messengers could change horses and carry on. Archaeologists believe the westernmost sections may have been built earlier by Assyrian kings.

An inscription in the tunnel tells how two teams cut their way through the rock from opposite ends until they met. The Siloam tunnel carries water 533 metres from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam in Jerusalem, and its ends differ by only 30 centimetres in height. The tunnel is most often linked to King Hezekiah of Judah, and the Bible mentions a tunnel he had built to bring water into the city. According to Wikipedia, radiocarbon samples from the plaster and datings of speleothems support that dating.

text.en: The most common dating is the time of King Hezekiah, the late 8th and early 7th century BC. After excavations in 2011 Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron instead suggested the late 9th or early 8th century BC, and they argue that Hezekiah’s waterworks in the Bible may have been somewhere else.

summary.en: FIFA, the world football federation, counts the Chinese ball game cuju among the earliest kicking games for which there is written evidence. A military work from the 3rd or 2nd century BC describes the game as an exercise. The first historical text to mention cuju, the Zhan Guo Ce, does so in its section on the state of Qi, and in Qi’s wealthy capital Linzi various forms of the game were played for entertainment. A competitive form was used to keep the cavalry fit, and under the Han dynasty matches were played at court on fields with six crescent-shaped goalposts at each end.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the military work to the 3rd or 2nd century BC, but says elsewhere that FIFA relies on a military manual from the Han dynasty, which began in 206 BC. The Zhan Guo Ce and Sima Qian’s chronicle are mentioned without dates.

summary.en: At Itazuke in Fukuoka archaeologists have found rice paddies, canals with a weir, carbonised rice and even human footprints. The site counts among the first in Japan with irrigated rice farming, although this is debated. Farming came to northern Kyushu from the Korean Peninsula, together with millet. The new farmers, whom archaeologists call the Yayoi people, were migrants from Korea and nearby regions who mixed with the Jōmon people already living on the islands.

text.en: The Yayoi period is traditionally dated to about 300 BC–AD 300. Radiocarbon datings of residues on potsherds point to about 1000–800 BC, up to 500 years earlier, but this is described as highly controversial. The article on Itazuke describes the paddies both as from the late Jōmon period and, judging by the pottery, as from the very beginning of the Yayoi culture.

summary.en: During the Bronze Age, Asian elephants lived far west of India. The finds range from at least 1800 BC to about 700 BC, when the elephants probably died out. Climatic shifts and new land use in the early Iron Age have been suggested as causes. Some scholars suspect that the animals had been brought there by people, perhaps from India, but this has not been shown.

Inside a large stone enclosure in the village of Balathal, a middle-aged man was buried in layers of ash from burnt cow dung. He lived in the Chalcolithic, and according to the researchers radiocarbon dates of the layers show that he was buried between 2500 and 2000 BC. The skeleton has lesions around the nose and upper jaw, in the joints and on the shinbone. When the researchers compared them with other diseases in 2009, they concluded that the man had lepromatous leprosy. They described the find as the oldest documented skeletal evidence for the disease.

In Cloggs Cave in Victoria, archaeologists have found two small fireplaces, each with a trimmed stick of Casuarina wood bearing traces of fat. They are about 12,000 and 11,000 years old. They resemble rituals that GunaiKurnai medicine men and women performed according to 19th-century ethnographers.

text.en: According to 19th-century ethnographers, caves among the GunaiKurnai were not homes but secluded places for the mulla-mullung, medicine men and women who could heal the sick but also harm an enemy with magic, among other ways with a small fire and a wooden stick smeared with fat. The excavation was carried out at the invitation of GunaiKurnai Elders. The researchers believe the custom was handed down for some 500 generations.

summary.en: At Mount Hora in northern Malawi, about 9,500 years ago, hunter-gatherers burned a dead adult, probably a woman, on a large pyre. Cut marks on the bones suggest that the flesh was removed first, and stone tools may have been placed in the pyre as grave offerings. According to Wikipedia, it is Africa’s oldest known cremation pyre.

text.en: The text is based on Wikipedia, and the point on the map is the mountain according to Wikidata; the rock shelter lies at its foot. The Wikipedia article is based on the study by Cerezo-Román et al. (2026), which is only linked here to check the date and place. The study dates the cremation to 9,540–9,454 calibrated years before present.

summary.en: On the bed of Lake Huron, 32 metres below the surface, there was dry land about 9,000 years ago. There archaeologists have found two flakes of obsidian from Wagontire in Oregon, more than 4,000 kilometres away. It is the oldest known find of obsidian in eastern North America, and the stone probably passed through many hands.

text.en: The article gives no coordinates for the find site. The point on the map is the centre of Lake Huron according to Wikipedia.

summary.en: At Gebel Ramlah in the Western Desert of southern Egypt, herders buried their dead in the fifth millennium BC with ornaments of Red Sea shells and mussels from the Nile. According to Wikipedia, the shells probably point to an exchange that reached the Red Sea coast, but the people may also have travelled there themselves.

In Porc-Epic Cave near Dire Dawa in eastern Ethiopia, Middle Stone Age hunters left behind obsidian tools. The stone is not found nearby but comes from three sources 150–250 kilometres away. According to Wikipedia, the stone material was obtained on journeys through the landscape or through exchange with neighbours.

text.en: The obsidian has not been dated on its own. The Middle Stone Age layers have been radiocarbon dated on snail opercula to about 41,000–37,000 years ago, and one sample is older than 43,000 radiocarbon years; a jawbone has been dated by another method to about 50,000 years. The use of ochre probably began about 45,000 years ago or earlier. The researchers write that the chronology is uncertain and that the layers may span a longer period. The span here runs from 50,000 to 37,000 years ago.

summary.en: Obsidian is a volcanic glass. At the site of Matenkupkum on New Ireland there was obsidian from the neighbouring island of New Britain at least 12,000 years ago, so the stone had been carried across the sea. According to Wikipedia, obsidian was traded in what is now Papua New Guinea at least 23,000 years ago. The sources differ on when the exchange began.

text.en: Roberts et al. (2022) show obsidian from New Britain at Matenkupkum at least 12,000 years ago and have also found traces of obsidian in dental calculus from there. Wikipedia writes that obsidian tools were traded at least 23,000 years ago. Gandini et al. (2025) write of obsidian exchange networks emerging from the end of the Pleistocene onwards. Shaw et al. (2020), only linked here as a check, write that obsidian from the Kutau deposit on the Willaumez Peninsula has been used for 24,000 years. The span here runs from 23,000 to 12,000 years ago. The point on the map is the centre of the island.

summary.en: Lake Victoria, Africa’s largest lake, is only 68–81 metres deep and has dried out completely at least three times, most recently during the last ice age. When the rains returned it filled again, first with wetlands and then with a deep lake. The sources differ on when this happened.

text.en: Wikipedia writes that the lake last dried out about 17,300 years ago and had refilled by 14,700 years ago, and elsewhere that it dried out about 15,000 years ago. Ngoepe et al. (2023) date the last complete desiccation to the coldest part of the last ice age, about 26,500–19,000 years ago, and write that the lake began to fill about 17,000 years ago and had shallow water and wetlands about 16,000 years ago. The sources also differ on the depth: Ngoepe et al. give 68 metres and Wikipedia 80–81 metres. The span here runs from 17,000 to 14,700 years ago.

summary.en: The Rotoiti eruption in the Ōkataina Caldera on New Zealand’s North Island threw out about 100 cubic kilometres of magma or more. Its ash and ignimbrite cover large parts of the northern North Island, and geologists use the layer as a reference layer in the stratigraphy. When the eruption happened is disputed.

text.en: The eruption is hard to date. The Wikipedia article on the Rotoiti Caldera gives about 50,000 years ago. The article on the Ōkataina Caldera gives about 55,000 years ago in one place and about 50,000 in another. The article on Lake Rotoiti writes that research has given anything from 64,000 to 40,000 years ago, and that 47,400 ± 1,500 years ago has been cited recently. According to the same article, a review of 27 dates (Hopkins et al. 2021) gave a consensus of about 55,000–45,000 years ago. The span here runs from 64,000 to 40,000 years ago. The eruption’s vents probably lay in the eastern part of Lake Rotoiti; the point on the map is the lake.

caption.en: Modern photo (2007) of Lake Rotoiti northeast of Lake Rotorua on the North Island, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: The Aitape Skull was found in 1929 inland from Sissano Lagoon on New Guinea’s north coast and is about 6,000 years old. A 2017 study concludes that it was carried there by a tsunami. The person may then be the oldest known tsunami victim, or may already have been buried when the wave came.

text.en: The study by Goff et al. (2017) states that the skull is about 6,000 years old, and Wikipedia gives 6,000–7,000 years. The Wikipedia article is largely based on the same study, so the sources are not independent. The point on the map is Sissano Lagoon; the find site lies about 12 kilometres inland.

summary.en: In the rock shelters of Laas Geel outside Hargeisa in Somaliland are vivid paintings of cattle, some in ceremonial robes, and of the herders who probably painted them. They are about 5,500–4,500 years old and are among the earliest known images of domestic cattle in the Horn of Africa.

caption.en: Modern photo (2012) of the rock paintings at Laas Geel, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In a rock shelter on the Gilf Kebir plateau in Egypt’s desert are paintings of people who seem to be swimming, and of a giraffe and a hippopotamus, among others. László Almásy found the site in 1933. The paintings may be as old as around 8000 BC, when the Sahara was greener. What they depict is disputed.

text.en: What the paintings depict is disputed. Almásy interpreted the figures as real swimmers. The German ethnologist Hans Rhotert was the first to see them as dead people, and the anthropologist Jean-Loïc Le Quellec agrees and compares them with the ancient Egyptian Coffin Texts, in which the souls of the dead float in the primeval waters of Nun. Andras Zboray doubts that the figures are swimming at all and calls them symbolic, with an unknown meaning. The dating is an estimate.

caption.en: Modern photo (2011) of the painting of swimmers in the Cave of Swimmers at Wadi Sura, Gilf Kebir, in Egypt’s Western Desert, not from the time of the event. Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In the cave of Guilá Naquitz in Oaxaca in southern Mexico, archaeologists have found remains of the squash Cucurbita pepo whose rinds and stalks grew thicker over time, a sign that people were selecting and growing the plant. According to Wikipedia, it is the oldest known evidence of a domesticated crop on the continent.

text.en: Wikipedia states that squash was domesticated 10,750–8,000 years ago. Early dates of about 10,000 years have been questioned, not because the measurements are wrong but because of what they show, and the first certain sign that people were selecting the squash is placed at about 8,000 years ago. The span here follows Wikipedia’s 10,750–8,000 years ago.

summary.en: The Nebra bronze disc has gold figures read as a sun or full moon, a crescent moon and stars, among them a group usually taken to be the Pleiades. No older concrete depiction of heavenly bodies is known anywhere. The disc belongs to the Únětice culture and was dug up by looters on the Mittelberg in 1999.

text.en: Wikipedia states that archaeologists date the disc to about 1800–1600 BC. Birch bark in the swords found with it has been radiocarbon dated to 1600–1560 BC, which dates the burial; by then the disc had probably existed for several generations. A 2020 paper proposed an Iron Age date instead, but another paper rejected its arguments the same year, and analyses of the disc and the find spot support the Bronze Age date.

summary.en: Nine craters on Saaremaa formed when a meteorite of 20–80 tonnes broke apart in the air and the pieces struck the ground. The largest, 110 metres wide, now holds Lake Kaali. Forest burned up to 6 km away, and the island was already inhabited. The lake is seen as a later cult site, where animal bones may be traces of sacrifices.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the most recent dating places the impact shortly after 1530–1450 BC, and the span here follows it. The same article says that estimates by different researchers vary by as much as 6,000 years, from about 6400 to 400 BC, and another section gives 1600–800 BC for when the lake formed.

summary.en: A clay vessel of the Vučedol culture, dated to about 2600 BC, was found in a Copper Age mound in the centre of Vinkovci. Its four bands of signs are read as the four seasons of the year, each with twelve boxes for signs in the sky, and according to this interpretation the calendar follows the constellation Orion.

text.en: The reading as a calendar comes from Wikipedia’s article on the Vučedol culture, which in its image captions refers to the archaeologist Aleksandar Durman’s article on celestial symbolism in the Vučedol culture (Documenta Praehistorica 28, 2001) and, for the dating, to an exhibition catalogue from the Croatian Ministry of Culture (2009). The sentences about Orion and about the bands and boxes have no citation in Wikipedia, and we have not been able to open Durman’s article. We have therefore not been able to check the interpretation in the research, so it should be read as an interpretation, not as an established fact.

summary.en: The Greek geographer Pytheas of Massalia travelled to northern Europe around 325 BC and visited much of the British Isles. He is the first person on record to describe the midnight sun, and he called the northern tip of Britain Orcas. His book is lost and is known only through later writers.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the voyage took place around 325 BC. Elsewhere the article says that the most that can be said with certainty is that it happened in the 320s BC or shortly after, and the name Orcas is assigned to 320 BC. The article also disagrees with itself about the route: the introduction says he circumnavigated and visited a considerable part of the British Isles, but a later section says that, if he took a certain route, in all likelihood he did not actually circumnavigate Britain.

summary.en: With about 7.3 km³ of ejected material, Hekla 3 is among Iceland’s largest eruptions since the last ice age. Ash from it has been found in Scottish peat bogs. The eruption may have cooled the northern hemisphere for a few years, and in Ireland trees hardly grew at all for a decade.

text.en: Wikipedia gives three dates for Hekla 3 in the same article: about 1000 BC in the text, 950 BC in the 2019 values and 1063 ± 140 BC in a newer calibration from 2024. The span here follows the last one, 1203–923 BC, which also includes the other two.

summary.en: The oaks in the Corlea road were felled in late 148 or early 147 BC, according to the tree rings. From split planks a road at least a kilometre long was built across the bog, wide enough for wheels. Within about ten years the bog had swallowed it. Its purpose is unknown.

A ship sank off Antikythera around 70–60 BC. Its cargo included a hand-cranked instrument with at least 30 bronze gears that could follow the Sun and the Moon and predict eclipses. It is often called the oldest known analogue computer. Sponge divers found the wreck in 1900.

text.en: Wikipedia’s article on the mechanism places the sinking at about 70–60 BC, and the article on the wreck in the second quarter of the 1st century BC. The mechanism itself has been dated in different ways: about 205 BC, 150–100 BC or about 87 BC. It was therefore built before the sinking, but how long before is disputed.

summary.en: The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis has been found in the teeth of three people who lived in Britain about 4,000 years ago: two children from a mass burial at Charterhouse Warren and a woman at Levens in Cumbria. They are the earliest traces of plague detected so far in Britain. How severe the disease was is unclear.

Speleothems from three caves in Germany and Austria show cooler weather and dry winters around 2250–2150 BC, during the so-called 4.2 event. In Spannagel Cave it is the coldest time in the 2,000 years the study covers. At the same time, the population in the northern Alpine foreland clearly declined.

Isotopes in bones and teeth show that a woman at Pielgrzymowice ate a lot of millet around 1590 BC, give or take 50 years, but not as a child. It is the earliest evidence of people in the area eating a lot of millet, and according to the study it pushes the oldest known millet eating in Europe back by more than a century.

A young person was buried alone at Valencina around 2900–2650 BC with, among other things, a whole African elephant tusk. The researchers argue that the grave goods make her the most prominent person on the peninsula in the Copper Age before the Bell Beaker culture. Proteins in the tooth enamel showed in 2021 that she was a woman, not a man.

A fortified wooden settlement was built on a wet island in a lake in northern Poland, today a peninsula. Tree rings show that the oaks were felled in 747–722 BC, most of them in the winter of 748/747 BC. The settlement belonged to the Lusatian culture. When it was found in 1933, it was first thought to be Slavic.

In the 1st century BC the Celtic Boii minted silver and gold coins where Bratislava stands today. The coins carry fourteen different inscriptions in Latin capitals, most often the name Biatec, presumably a king. No older writing is known in Slovakia or the neighbouring lands.

Salt was mined at Hallstatt already in the Bronze Age, and from the 8th century BC until about 500 BC the Alpine mines were the centre of a wealthy community whose prosperity shows in the cemeteries. In the mine tunnels the salt has preserved leather, wood and textiles, among them backpacks. The place gave its name to the Hallstatt culture.

With tools of stone and bone, people began mining copper ore on the Great Orme in north Wales about 4,000 years ago. Around 1600 BC it was the only working copper mine in Britain, and it was at its most productive in 1700–1400 BC. In total up to 1,760 tonnes of copper may have been mined.

A painted stucco relief from the palace of Knossos, from about 1450–1400 BC, shows a person upside down over a bull’s back, with one figure at the animal’s horns and one behind it. Bull-leaping is a common motif in Minoan art. Whether it was a sport, a ceremony or both is debated.

In the valley where Thracian rulers were buried, near Kazanlak, a small domed brick tomb was built in the 4th century BC. Its frescoes show a couple at a ritual funeral feast, with musicians, horses and a chariot. No paintings from the Hellenistic period are better preserved in Bulgaria. The tomb has been a World Heritage Site since 1979.

On the summit of Tatićev Kamen near Kokino there are traces of people from the 19th to the 7th century BC, most of them from the Middle Bronze Age. Vessels with offerings were placed in cracks in the rock, so the site is interpreted as a holy mountain. Its discoverers believe that stones there marked the sunrise at the solstices.

text.en: The interpretation of Kokino as a megalithic observatory was put forward in 2002 by its discoverers. When the site was nominated for UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2011, the nomination was rejected, because the number of possible observation points and markers means that the alignments with the Sun could be due to chance.

summary.en: On the tombolo at Cape Trafalgar, archaeologists have excavated two Bronze Age megalithic tombs. Radiocarbon dating shows that they were used mainly around 1875–1600 BC. They may have been built then, and if so they are among the last megalithic tombs in the Iberian Peninsula. The grave goods include gold, silver and ivory.

Around 1650–1250 BC the thylacine vanished from mainland Australia, and the Tasmanian devil at about the same time. Both lived on in Tasmania. The dingo appeared on the mainland in the same period, and researchers name it, a growing population and a changing climate as possible causes.

text.en: The article on the thylacine says that the species died out on the mainland 3,600–3,200 years ago. The youngest dates are about 3,500 years old, and the estimated time is about 3,200 years ago. The article on the Tasmanian devil gives about 3,500 years ago. Rock paintings in Arnhem Land may be less than 1,000 years old, so the thylacine may have survived longer in some place, but this is uncertain.

caption.en: Thylacine skeletons, photographed at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery in Hobart. Modern photo (2018), not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: The youngest known bone of Sylviornis comes from the Pindai Caves and is dated to 1120–840 BC. The bird lived only in New Caledonia, could not fly, stood about 80 cm tall and weighed 27–34 kg. Its bones are often found at sites used by people, and the Lapita people probably hunted it until it died out.

At seven early settlement sites, five in Vanuatu and two in Fiji, there are bones of a large hornless tortoise that lived on land. Many bones are burnt and bear cut marks from butchery. In Vanuatu they date to around 1050–750 BC. People hunted the tortoises until the species died out.

text.en: The researchers only tentatively place the tortoise in the genus Meiolania and therefore write the species name with a question mark: ?Meiolania damelipi.

summary.en: Pago is a young volcanic cone inside the Witori Caldera on New Britain. Around 1370 BC, with an uncertainty of a hundred years, the volcano had one of its largest eruptions. Of the three large eruptions the source lists, it produced the most material: about 30 cubic kilometres of ash and rock (VEI 6).

According to earlier research, El Niño grew stronger from around 2050 BC. A sediment core from Girraween Lagoon shows a drier and more changeable climate at that time. Around 1050 BC the traces of fire change. Aboriginal people probably then began managing the landscape with fire, or did so more, perhaps because of the climate or a growing population.

Watom Island has Lapita pottery from before 1050 BC. Yet two people buried there around 750–250 BC had only Papuan ancestry in their DNA, closest to Baining speakers on New Britain. Isotopes suggest that they grew up on the island. East Asian ancestry is found in a person from around AD 50.

text.en: The study contradicts itself. In the text, the two people with only Papuan ancestry are dated to around 750–250 BC. In the table of individuals, one of them has 741–161 BC, and the other's date (1881–1421 BC) is struck out as unreliable. The researchers themselves point out that the interpretation rests on only five individuals from a long period.

summary.en: In the Ucheliungs burial cave in Palau's limestone islands, two people have been dated to around 975–546 BC. They and 19 others up to around AD 1450 had about 60 per cent East Asian and 40 per cent Papuan ancestry, like Palauans today. According to the study, this is the longest known continuity in Remote Oceania.

Graves on the island of Uripiv show how diet changed from the Lapita period, around 850–550 BC, to the time after it, around 550–50 BC. Isotopes in the skeletons show more and more food from the land and less from the sea, which fits with farming growing. Three people from the later period had probably moved there after childhood.

Kava is a plant whose root is ground and mixed with water to make a drink used at ceremonies around the Pacific. It was probably developed by growers in northern Vanuatu about 3,000 years ago, around 1050 BC, by selecting from the wild species Piper wichmannii. The cultivated varieties are sterile and are propagated without seeds.

The diet of the Aboriginal people of Tasmania seems to have changed around 2050 BC: more possums, kangaroos and wallabies and almost no scaled fish. They also appear to have replaced bone tools with sharp stone tools. The reason is disputed. One explanation is that scrubland turned into grassland that gave more other food.

In a waste layer in a small building in an Iron Age village near Aalborg lay bones of a bicoloured shrew, a species not among Denmark's shrews today. DNA revealed the species, and a jawbone was dated to around 900–570 BC. The researchers lean towards it having lived there, but cannot rule out that it was carried there.

Just over 500 analyses of metal objects show that more and more metal reached southern Scandinavia from around 2100–2000 BC, first from the Inn Valley in Austria and Slovakia via central Germany. Around 1500 BC British copper no longer appears in the finds, and in 1450–1300 BC over 60 per cent of the samples point to northern Italy.

Mortensnes on the Varanger Fjord was a large settlement for thousands of years. Yet DNA and pollen from a nearby lake show that it noticeably affected the plants around it only in the last 3,600 years or so, through grazing, and more in the last thousand years, probably through reindeer herding and possibly domestic stock.

Ajvide on Gotland was a settlement of hunter-gatherers of the Pitted Ware culture. In DNA from skeletons found there, researchers detected traces of the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis (meningococci). In one person who lived around 2800 BC the find counts as a probable case, in another as ambiguous.

Fat residues in pottery show that around 2500 BC people in southern Finland went from food from the water to products from ruminants. At three Corded Ware sites in Kirkkonummi there was ruminant fat, and in three beakers milk fat. This shows livestock farming that far north. Dairying probably came with a new population.

Near Pattijoki, a stone enclosure of about 60 by 35 metres was built around 2000 BC, with walls seven metres wide and six openings. It then stood on a rocky shore, and more than twenty stone cairns surround it. The source does not say what it was for, but pits nearby may have stored killed game.

Around 800–400 BC a settlement with wooden houses stood on the Lithuanian coast. Bronze was cast in moulds there, and amber and working waste turn up across almost the whole excavation. As Lithuania has no metal ore, researchers link the amber to trade. People grew barley, peas, lentils and broad beans, and mostly kept domestic animals.

Bones from sites in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania show that porpoises were fairly numerous in the eastern Baltic 6,000–4,000 years ago. After around 3000 BC they seem to have become fewer, as the sea also became less salty. At Sārnate in Latvia people appear to have stamped patterns into pots with porpoise jaws.

Around 1000 BC people in eastern Lithuania began to build fortified settlements on hills, with rectangular post houses. Each settlement is thought to have housed about 80–120 people. They hunted, gathered and kept sheep, pigs and cattle but farmed less. At some sites metal was cast in clay moulds.

Olbia was a Greek colony from Miletus on the Southern Bug estuary. Grain, fish and slaves were shipped from here to Greece. In the 5th century BC the city cast bronze money, including coins shaped like leaping dolphins, when most Greek coins were otherwise round and struck.

Dental calculus from people buried at Bilsk and Mamai-Gora in Ukraine around 700–200 BC contained proteins from the milk of cattle, sheep and goats. One person also had protein from horse milk. The sample is small: six of eleven people with reliable samples had milk proteins.

Copper mining began at Kargaly in the southern Urals around 3000 BC. After a long break around 2500–1900 BC it became far more intensive and went on until about 1400 BC. The area covers almost 500 km², with up to 35,000 traces of shafts, galleries and open pits.

text.en: In one place the source says mining began at the end of the 4th millennium BC or at the turn of the 3rd, that is around 3000 BC, and in another that the earliest period belongs to the second half of the 4th millennium BC (3500–3000 BC). Around 3000 BC is shown here.

summary.en: In the first quarter of the 3rd century BC, Greeks from the Bosporus founded the town of Tanais in the Don delta. Strabo calls it a shared market for the nomads of Asia and Europe. They brought slaves, hides and animal products and received clothing and wine. Most of the amphora stamps from the excavations come from Rhodes.

In 122 BC Etna had a very violent explosive eruption from its summit, of the kind called Plinian. Tephra fell to the south-east, including on the town of Catania, where many roofs collapsed. The Roman government then exempted the people of Catania from taxes for ten years.

The Terramare culture of the Po plain left over 60 known villages, where people grew wheat, barley and legumes and kept livestock. Around 1200–1150 BC most villages south of the Po were abandoned. Possible causes mentioned are overpopulation, depleted resources and periods of drought, but the causes are not fully clear.

The natural philosopher Alcmaeon of Croton lived around 500 BC. He saw health as a balance between opposing powers in the body and disease as one of them taking over. He placed thought in the head. A late antique source says he dissected, but whether he did, and if so on animals or humans, is disputed.

text.en: The English Wikipedia places his activity in the 5th century BC and calls a birth year of about 510 BC an estimate. The German Wikipedia says he lived in the late 6th and early 5th centuries BC, but also mentions that scholars have suggested he was active only after the middle of the 5th century BC. Around 500 BC is shown here.

summary.en: Archimedes lived in Syracuse on Sicily, around 287–212 BC. In his work On Floating Bodies he wrote that a body in a fluid is pushed upwards with a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Using polygons with 96 sides, he showed that π lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7.

By a stream near the Euphrates, in the foothills of the Taurus Mountains, people built a cult building into the slope around 8400–8100 BC. It had single-piece pillars and limestone sculptures, among them a head larger than life. Small clay figurines are interpreted as offerings. The site is now under water.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the site to 8400–8100 BC from flint tools and building style, and three radiocarbon dates point to the second half of the ninth millennium BC. A fourth date falls in the tenth millennium BC; if it is correct, there was an even earlier phase here. The site was excavated in 1983–1991 before the Atatürk Dam was filled.

summary.en: Eridu was founded around 5400 BC, in the Ubaid period, on a sand dune where no one had lived before. The Sumerians’ own texts make Eridu the first city, and it is traditionally counted as the oldest in southern Mesopotamia. The temple of the god Enki was rebuilt again and again on top of the older buildings.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the founding as around 5400 BC in the text and as 5500–5300 BC in the infobox. The number of temples built on top of each other is given as 18 in one place and as 17 in another.

summary.en: Around 4100–4000 BC, grapes were pressed in a cave by the Arpa River in Armenia. There is a clay pressing basin, a vat for fermentation, large jars and remains of grape seeds and skins. Traces of a pigment from red wine show that it was wine. It is the oldest known site of winemaking.

text.en: The cave was excavated in 2007–2010 under the direction of Boris Gasparyan, and the dating is based on radiocarbon. According to Wikipedia, the installation’s closeness to graves suggests that the wine may have been used at burials or offerings, but this is an inference, not a certain finding. Who built it is not known.

summary.en: More than a thousand mustatils, long courtyards within sandstone walls, are found in north-western Saudi Arabia. A chamber in the middle of one of them held only pieces of cattle skulls. Radiocarbon on the pieces shows that it was built around 5300–5000 BC, and perhaps the others too. The finds are believed to be traces of an unknown cult.

Barnacles on flakes of bitumen show that boats made their way out on the Persian Gulf from site H3 in Kuwait in the second half of the sixth millennium BC. The other side of the flakes bears reed impressions: the bitumen sealed boats of bundled reeds. The finds are described as the oldest known traces of boats at sea.

text.en: The site is dated by its pottery, which resembles vessels from Mesopotamia’s Ubaid period (Ubaid 2–3), and by a single radiocarbon date from the oldest layer: 5511–5324 BC. The excavations began in 1998 and were directed by Harriet Crawford.

summary.en: During the last ice age the sea level was at its lowest about 125 metres lower than today, and most of the floor of the Persian Gulf was land: a plain where rivers met. When the ice melted, the sea rose, and the gulf became a sea about 12,000–6,000 years ago. The plain may have been a refuge for people.

text.en: The article gives two time statements: that the sea began to fill the basin about 15,000 years ago, and that the present sea formed as the sea level rose about 12,000–6,000 years ago. The span here follows the latter. When the sea reached its present level is not stated.

summary.en: Kot Diji, opposite Mohenjo-daro on the Indus, has given its name to a culture of the Early Harappan phase. The site is estimated to have been inhabited from around 3300 BC. The elite lived on a height behind a wall with bastions, and below lay mud-brick houses on stone foundations. The whole site shows traces of large fires.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the site was inhabited from around 3300 BC, and the culture is dated to 3300–2800 BC in one place and to 3300–2600 BC in another. At the same time the lowest layer, Kot Diji I, is given as 2605 BC. Why the fires came and the site was abandoned is not explained.

summary.en: In north-western Tajikistan lay Sarazm, which is described as the first city in Central Asia with economic ties in a network of places, from the Turkmen steppes and the Aral Sea to the Iranian Plateau and the Indus. The pottery shows contacts in several directions, and the inhabitants worked metal on the site.

text.en: Most researchers have the settlement begin in the first half of the fourth millennium BC, but Wikipedia writes that the layers are uncertainly dated. The radiocarbon dates span roughly 3900–2100 BC, and two series give different answers: the oldest layer is dated to about 3907–3645 BC in one and to 3350–2890 BC in the other.

summary.en: Liangzhu was the centre of a culture in the Yangtze Delta known for its jade. The city had clay walls with water and land gates. High dams were built north-west of it and low ones on the plain, the latter of clay in bundles of grass. The water system is counted as the oldest known in the world on such a large scale.

text.en: The culture and the city are given as around 3300–2300 BC, but the article’s table gives the city as about 3000–2300 BC. The high dams are given as about 3100–2600 BC and the low ones as about 3000–2600 BC. Why the culture disappeared is not certain; several researchers point to floods.

summary.en: On the hills at Niuheliang, during the Hongshan culture around 3500–3000 BC, there was a place for burials and offerings where no dwellings have been found. A clay head with jade eyes gave an underground complex with painted walls the name Goddess Temple. There is also an altar and burial cairns.

text.en: The name Goddess Temple comes from the Chinese archaeologists and is based on the find of the clay head; it is not a certain identification of what the complex was used for. Wikipedia dates the Hongshan culture to 4700–2900 BC, while Niuheliang itself is given as 3500–3000 BC.

summary.en: Chemical analyses of jars from the village of Jiahu in Henan gave signs of a fermented drink of rice, honey and hawthorn and/or grapes. The jars date from about 7000–5500 BC. The researchers assume that mould broke the rice down into sugar before fermentation, and the drink was flavoured with flowers and resin.

text.en: Wikipedia names rice, honey and hawthorn leaves in its introduction and rice, honey, grapes and hawthorn further down; that is why hawthorn and/or grapes is given here. The analysis was made by a group led by Patrick McGovern. The dates follow the group’s 2004 study, in which the sherds come from the village’s three oldest periods, about 7000–5500 BC; the study is only linked.

summary.en: At Kakinoshima, in what is now the city of Hakodate on Hokkaido, archaeologists have found red-lacquered objects that are about 9,000 years old. They are described as the oldest known lacquerwork in the world. The site was inhabited in the Jōmon period, from around 7000 to 1000 BC.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the lacquer objects are about 9,000 years old, citing Crawford (2011), but does not say how they were dated.

summary.en: Kikai Caldera lies almost entirely under the sea south of Kyushu. About 7,300–7,200 years ago it exploded with a strength of 7 on the VEI scale. Glowing flows of ash and rock reached the coast about 100 kilometres away, and ash fell as far as Hokkaido. The eruption hit the Jōmon culture of southern Kyushu hard.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the eruption as about 7,200–7,300 years ago and elsewhere as 7,300 years ago. The article also writes that the consequences for the Jōmon culture may have been smaller than some have claimed, since a pottery tradition from before the eruption lived on in Kyushu.

summary.en: Kurile Lake in southern Kamchatka fills a caldera that formed in an enormous eruption in 6460–6414 BC. About 140–170 cubic kilometres of material were thrown out, and the ash settled over more than two million square kilometres. It is the largest known eruption in Kamchatka since the Ice Age.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the eruption as 6460–6414 BC. A study that the article refers to gives 7,600 radiocarbon years before present, which is a different way of counting and cannot be compared directly. “Since the Ice Age” here means the Holocene, the period the article refers to.

summary.en: About 42,000 years ago a woolly mammoth calf, only 30–35 days old, died on what is now the Yamal Peninsula. She is believed to have got stuck in deep mud as the herd crossed a riverbed and to have suffocated on the mud she breathed in. Reindeer herders found her in 2007, so well preserved that her mother’s milk was still in her stomach.

text.en: Wikipedia only states that the calf was found near the Yuribey River on the Yamal Peninsula, without an exact find site. The point on the map is the river’s mouth in Baydaratskaya Bay according to Wikidata. The article gives the age as about 42,000 years without saying how it was calculated.

summary.en: In a limestone cave on Borneo, 31,500–30,400 years ago, a young adult was buried who lacked the lower part of the left lower leg. The cut surfaces are clean and have healed, and the researchers conclude that the leg was removed by surgery, probably in childhood. The person then lived at least 6–9 more years.

text.en: The grave is radiocarbon dated on charcoal to 31,519–30,437 years before present, and a tooth by another method to 25,400 ± 4,300 years. The researchers rule out an accident and an animal attack and write that it is not known whether the operation was a rare exception. The study gives no coordinates.

summary.en: The village of Bhirrana in Haryana lies by the old channels of the seasonal Ghaggar River. The lowest layer has pit dwellings, Hakra ware and objects of smelted copper, and later a settlement with a wall and houses with several rooms grew up in the heyday of the Indus Valley. How old the lowest layers are is disputed.

text.en: Half a dozen charcoal samples from the early levels, analysed in 2004–2005, gave 3200–2600 BC, and the timeline follows them. Two other charcoal samples from the oldest layers have been dated to 7570–7180 and 6689–6201 BC. The excavators (Rao 2005) propose 7500–6000 BC, another researcher 6000–3800 BC, and the type of pottery points to the later part of the fourth millennium BC. The archaeologist Gregory Possehl has questioned the datings. According to Wikipedia the site was abandoned around 2500 BC.

summary.en: Along Norway’s continental shelf, huge masses of sediment slid into the deep in three large slides. The last one took place around 6225–6170 BC, according to carbon in the tsunami deposits. The wave left sand up to 29 km inland in Scotland. What set off the slides is debated.

text.en: Everything comes from one article. It mentions two explanations: an earthquake that made methane hydrate expand, or layers of sediment from the Ice Age; the latter is called the prevailing conclusion. That the tsunami killed up to a quarter of Britain’s population is an estimate.

summary.en: Where the Baltic Sea lies today, a large meltwater lake existed after the Ice Age. About 11,620 years ago it broke through a narrow passage at Billingen in Västergötland and fell to sea level, in several steps over half a year to a year and a half. Then salt water could flow in, and the Yoldia Sea followed.

text.en: The article gives the end as 11,620 calibrated years before 1950; older works used other dates. How long the outflow lasted is now put at half a year to a year and a half, but some researchers think it took decades. The 1920s picture of a single great outburst no longer holds.

summary.en: About 13,000 years ago, the volcano at Laacher See in the Eifel erupted violently, on roughly the same scale as Pinatubo in 1991. Ash fell over more than 300,000 km², from central France to Poland and southern Sweden. The deposits dammed the Rhine until the dam broke and the flood reached Bonn.

text.en: The article gives two estimates: 12,880 ± 40 years before 1950 and 13,006 ± 9 calibrated years before 1950, the latter from a radiocarbon date published in 2021. A 2023 paper argues that carbon dioxide from the magma may have affected the new date.

summary.en: About 39,200–39,700 years ago, Campi Flegrei near Naples produced the largest explosive volcanic eruption in Europe in 200,000 years. Ash fell over about three million km². Model calculations suggest Western Europe was 2–4 degrees colder for one to two years, but no certain trace of the eruption has been found in polar ice.

text.en: The span comes from radiocarbon dating. The argon–argon method gives 39,850 ± 140 years, and the article says the methods differ by a few centuries. The article on Campi Flegrei gives 39,280 ± 110 years and an older estimate of about 37,000 years.

summary.en: A man of about 25, found in the Villabruna rock shelter in northern Italy and dated to about 14,200–13,800 years ago, had a large cavity in a wisdom tooth. Scratches in the hole suggest that someone scraped it out with pointed flint tools while he was alive. The researchers see it as a sign of knowledge about treating disease.

text.en: Everything about the find comes from one study (Oxilia et al. 2015). The man was directly dated in older studies that the article refers to. No trace of any medicine in the hole could be shown, and the starch found there was probably contamination.

summary.en: At Champ-Durand in western France, the skull of a cow from around 3400–3000 BC has been found with a hole in the frontal bone. The marks around the hole resemble those on human skulls operated on by scraping, and the bone never healed. Perhaps people wanted to save the animal, perhaps they practised on it before operating on humans.

text.en: The study (Ramirez Rozzi and Froment 2018) dates the settlement to 3400–3000 BC, but its conclusion says the practice already existed in 4000 BC, which does not match that span. An earlier study (Braguier 1999) suggested that the hole came from another cow’s horn; that interpretation is rejected. The researchers also raise the possibility that the cow was already dead when the hole was made.

summary.en: For some 35,000 years, until around 3000 BC, people took refuge in Franchthi Cave in Argolis. Obsidian from the island of Melos turns up in the cave from as far back as about 13,000 BC. The finds are counted as early evidence of seafaring in Greece.

Sesklo in Thessaly has given its name to a farming culture, about 7510–4400 BC, which the article counts as the earliest known Neolithic culture in Europe. Around 5000 BC the village had 500–800 houses on about 20 hectares. How many lived there is unclear: 1,000–5,000 according to different researchers.

text.en: The start is the oldest dating: according to the article, about 7510–6190 BC applies to the oldest fragments (proto- and pre-Sesklo), and it gives neither a method nor a source for this. How the period ended is disputed: according to one theory, people from Dimini conquered the site around 5000 BC; according to another, the groups lived side by side for a time.

summary.en: During the fourth millennium BC, some settlements of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture, in present-day Ukraine, grew to more than 100 hectares. Talianky had 1,600–2,000 houses and Maidanetske almost 3,000. Researchers disagree on how many lived there at once, whether people only gathered there for parts of the year, and whether the sites were towns.

text.en: Population estimates range from a few thousand to 46,000 people, but the highest figure, for Maidanetske, appears to have been withdrawn. The number of houses does not show how many stood at the same time. The article on Talianky calls only the settlement there the largest known in Europe in the Neolithic.

summary.en: During the fifth millennium BC, people of the Vinča culture mined copper ore at Rudna Glava in eastern Serbia. The miners dug shafts into the slope and put up scaffolds to get at the ore. The site is among the earliest evidence of copper mining and metalworking in Europe.

text.en: The article on Rudna Glava gives only the fifth millennium BC and says the pottery shows that the site belongs to the Vinča culture. That only part of the ore was smelted and that the metal mostly became ornaments comes from the article on the Vinča culture, which thinks the ore was usually used as powder.

summary.en: At Gavà in Catalonia, people dug mines for variscite, a green mineral made into ornaments. The mines are dated to about 4200–3400 BC, but variscite from them is found in older graves in Huesca, so mining probably began earlier. They are the only known Neolithic variscite mines.

text.en: The dates from the mines are uncalibrated and, converted, become 4200–3400 BC. The samples come from fill that ended up there only after the mines were no longer used. Variscite chemically linked to Gavà has been found in graves from the sixth millennium BC in the Chaves and Moro caves in Huesca, and in Can Sadurní cave with dates older than those of Gavà.

summary.en: On the fells around Great Langdale in the Lake District, people knapped rough stone axe blanks around 4000–3500 BC. The axes were often polished elsewhere and have been found all over Britain and Ireland. About 27 per cent of the polished stone axes examined in Britain come from here.

text.en: The article dates the site to about 4000–3500 BC but also says that radiocarbon dates suggest it was used for about 1,000 years. The extent of the axe workshops is still being investigated.

summary.en: At Spiennes near Mons in Belgium, flint was mined from around 4300 to 2200 BC. The shafts went more than ten metres down and led to underground cavities. The flint became axe blanks, which were carried up to 150 km away and often polished there. The mines became a World Heritage Site in 2000.

When the A28 motorway was built in 1955, a hollowed-out pine log, just under three metres long, was found south of Pesse in the Netherlands. According to radiocarbon dating it was made between about 8040 and 7510 BC. It is described as the world’s oldest known boat. Some have doubted it was a boat, but a replica could be paddled.

At Morasko on the northern edge of Poznań there are seven craters left by meteorite impacts, and five of them hold small lakes. The largest is about 100 m across and 11 m deep. The impact is estimated to have happened about 5,000 years ago.

text.en: The age comes from Wikipedia, which refers to a luminescence dating (Stankowski et al. 2007). That study could not be opened, and the article gives only about 5,000 years.

summary.en: In southern Spain lay Los Millares, a Copper Age settlement used from around 3025 to 2000 BC. It was protected by three rings of stone walls, the outermost with 19 bastions. A large building shows traces of copper smelting. Probably about 1,000 people lived here.

text.en: The article gives 3025–2000 BC but elsewhere 3200–2300 BC. According to radiocarbon dating, one of the walls collapsed and was rebuilt around 3025 BC, so the settlement may be older than that.
