summary.en: On Gozo in Malta, Ġgantija was built around 3600 BC and used until around 2500 BC: two temples of large stone blocks and a third that was never finished. Figurines and statues from the site are linked to a fertility cult. The temples are older than the pyramids of Egypt and became a World Heritage Site in 1980.

text.en: The article gives 3600–2500 BC for the temples, but the Ġgantija phase, named after the site, is given on the same page as 3600–3200 BC. The southern temple is dated to around 3600 BC.

summary.en: At Ilumetsa in southeastern Estonia there are two hollows, about 75–80 and 50 metres across and 725 metres apart. Charcoal beneath what is thought to be ejected material shows that both formed at the same time, about 7,000–7,170 years ago. They are counted as probable meteorite craters, but this has not been proven.

text.en: Everything comes from one article. No certain pieces of a meteorite and no traces of shock metamorphism have been found; the idea of an impact rests on deformed layers and on the two forming at the same time. A radiocarbon date from the lowest layers gives about 6,660–7,170 years.

summary.en: A violent explosive eruption around 8000 BC blasted away the summit of the Ulleungdo volcano, leaving a caldera behind. The island lies 120 km east of the Korean Peninsula and is the part of a large stratovolcano on the seabed that reaches above the waves. Within the caldera, later eruptions raised the peak of Albong.

text.en: Date and text come only from Wikipedia, which gives neither the method nor whether the year is calibrated. The Nari Basin, part of the caldera, is today the island’s only flat ground.

summary.en: Seongsan Ilchulbong on Jeju is a tuff cone some 6,700 years old, built up by hydrovolcanic eruptions of the Surtseyan kind where the sea floor lay close to the surface. It rises 182 metres and measures 600 metres across. Since 2007 it has belonged to the World Heritage Site Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes.

At the site of Gosan-ri on Jeju, and at Ubong-ri near Ulsan, there are clay vessels from Korea’s earliest period with pottery. They are dated to around 8000 BC or earlier. According to Wikipedia, Korea’s Palaeolithic ended when people began making pottery.

text.en: Wikipedia’s page on prehistoric Korea gives around 8000 BC or earlier. The page on the Jeulmun period mentions estimates of around 10,000 BC and a date of 10,180 ± 65 radiocarbon years before present, without saying whether it is calibrated, but also later dates. The researcher Kuzmin, whom the page cites, holds that more dates are needed.

summary.en: Around 4000 BC the people of Amsa-dong, now part of Seoul, made their homes in umjip, huts with lowered floors. The finds point to cooked grain and fish in their diet by about 3000 BC. It is the only known major Stone Age site in Seoul and has been a protected historic site since 1979.

text.en: At one point the article says that the site was inhabited 3,000–4,000 years ago, which does not match the dates of around 4000 and 3000 BC given elsewhere in the same article.

summary.en: At Sakhtysh, hunter-gatherer-fishers buried their dead around 4850–2850 BC. Ancient DNA shows traces of hepatitis B virus in five of those studied and parvovirus B19 in four. Their immune-system genes were unusually alike, probably because the group was small and met few kinds of pathogens.

text.en: Date and text come only from one study (Genome Biology 2026); Wikidata gives only the point. The study examined individuals from the Lyalovo and Volosovo cultures. It also found DNA from the bacterium Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a possible infection from animals, in two teeth.

summary.en: At Lake Sindor, about 1,200 km northeast of Moscow, fragments of objects resembling skis have been found. They are dated to around 6300–5000 BC. Wikipedia counts them as the oldest known fragments of ski-like objects.

text.en: The information comes only from Wikipedia, which cites a 1985 article on Mesolithic wooden artefacts from the site of Vis I. Wikipedia also mentions skis from around 6000 BC in Karelia, with a news article as its source.

summary.en: On the middle Volga lived hunters and fishers with seasonal camps where rivers meet. From around 6700 BC they shaped pots from the mud of stagnant ponds and fired them in open fires at 450–600 °C. Wikipedia counts the pots as Europe’s oldest pottery.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the culture to the 7th millennium BC and the pots from 6700 BC onwards. That this is Europe’s oldest pottery rests on a 2010 book that the article cites. That the craft of pottery spread from here towards the Balkans is given only as a belief.

summary.en: At the Zamostje 2 site, hunter-gatherer-fishers cooked guelder rose berries together with freshwater fish in their clay pots around 5700–5300 BC. The berries are bitter and mildly toxic raw, and the fish may have made them more palatable. Later pots from the site show far fewer traces of the berries.

text.en: The results come from a study of food crusts in pots from 13 sites in northern and eastern Europe (PLOS ONE 2026). That guelder rose berries occur in the crusts from Zamostje 2 had also been shown in earlier studies that it cites. The site was also used in 4500–3500 BC.

summary.en: After the Ice Age, Ladoga was at first part of the Baltic Ice Lake. Between 9,500 and 9,100 years before present it belonged to the Ancylus Lake, a forerunner of the Baltic Sea. When the level of the Ancylus Lake fell, around 8,800 years before present (the source does not say whether these are radiocarbon years), Ladoga became a lake of its own.

text.en: Wikipedia does not say whether these years are radiocarbon or calendar years; for the melting of the ice it explicitly gives radiocarbon years. The information on the Ancylus Lake rests on a 1995 study that the article cites.

summary.en: In four cemeteries on the Angara River near Lake Baikal, the plague bacterium has been found in 18 hunter-gatherers. A first outbreak took place around 3570–3315 BC and a second a few centuries later. The disease struck small family groups and appears to have killed quickly, especially children.

text.en: Date and text come only from one study (Nature 2026); Wikidata gives only the point. The second outbreak is dated to 5,315–4,235 years before present, most likely 5,050–4,850. According to the study the plague bacterium arose before about 5,700 years ago; according to earlier studies that it cites, it could cause bubonic plague only from about 3,800 years ago.

summary.en: At the end of the Ice Age a glacier dammed a lake in the Chuya and Kuray basins in the Altai, holding up to 600 cubic kilometres of water behind an ice dam about 650 metres high. According to some geomorphologists the dam burst and the water rushed out along the Katun. Current ripples up to 18 metres high remain.

text.en: The article gives both 15,000–12,000 years ago and 12000–9000 BC, which do not fully agree. It says that the timing of the various floods is not firmly established and gives no dating method.

summary.en: In 2020 the frozen mummy of a three-week-old cub of the sabre-toothed cat Homotherium latidens was found by the Badyarikha River in Yakutia. Its wool is dated to about 37,000–35,500 years before present. Pollen and plant remains suggest that it lived in larch forest and moist meadows by a river.

text.en: The information comes from a study of the habitat at the find site (Scientific Reports 2025). The cub itself was described in an earlier 2024 article that the study cites. The radiocarbon date was made on the wool and gave 31,808 ± 367 radiocarbon years before present, which calibrates to 35,471–37,019 years before present.

summary.en: In the permafrost at Tumat in Yakutia a mummified wolf puppy was found with a piece of woolly rhinoceros tissue in its stomach. Both are dated to about 14,400 years ago, shortly before the species died out. The genome shows no inbreeding, and the researchers think the species vanished quickly.

text.en: The genome is analysed in one study (Genome Biology and Evolution 2026). That the species died out about 14,000 years ago, and that the tissue in the wolf’s stomach came from a rhinoceros, rests on earlier studies that it cites.

summary.en: Charred scraps of rope, netting and woven cloth have come to light in Chertovy Vorota Cave in the Sikhote-Alin mountains, lying under the remains of a wooden building that had burnt down. Dates taken on the textiles themselves place them about 9,400–8,400 years before present, and they were probably made from a sedge, Carex sordida.

text.en: Wikipedia does not say whether the years are calibrated. It describes the finds as the earliest textile remains in East Asia and cites a 2012 study in Antiquity. Since no spindle whorls were found, the researchers think the fabrics were made by hand or on a warp-weighted loom.

summary.en: According to a 2020 study, the people of the Fa-Hien Lena cave in Sri Lanka had the bow and arrow from at least 48,000 to 34,000 calibrated years before present. According to the study, this is the earliest evidence of the bow and arrow outside Africa.

text.en: The text is based on Wikipedia and the study's dates. The study (Langley et al. 2020) is licensed CC BY-NC and is used only for dates and place; no text is copied. Wikipedia also says that radiocarbon dates show the cave was occupied from about 33,000 years ago, which does not fit the study's 48,000 years.

summary.en: The dry Ghaggar–Hakra channel was once the course of the Sutlej River. Dates from river sand show that the large flow began to stop 15,000–12,000 years ago and was gone shortly after 8,000 years ago. The cities of the Indus Civilisation thus grew up in an abandoned valley, probably fed by monsoon rivers.

text.en: The ages are luminescence (OSL) dates on feldspar. The source gives them in thousands of years without saying from which year they are counted; here they are counted from 1950. At Kalibangan the large flow stopped between about 23,000 and 12,300 years ago, and in the middle reach of the valley only about 8,000 years ago. The researchers cannot say why the river changed course.

summary.en: At Lahuradewa on the Ganges Plain, rice has been found in the oldest layers, which have been radiocarbon dated to the 7th millennium BC. The finds have been interpreted as early cultivated rice. Other researchers think the rice was rather gathered wild and that the dates may be too old.

text.en: The historian Irfan Habib calls the early date for cultivated rice dubious; according to him, four of five radiocarbon dates from the oldest period lie between 4220 and 2879 BC. The archaeobotanist Dorian Fuller sees wild rice gathering as more likely and warns that early dates on the Ganges Plain may come from old wood. One source (Wikipedia).

summary.en: During the last ice age, sea level was at its lowest 120 metres below today's, and the Palk Strait was land between India and Sri Lanka. According to the article, the sea rose during the Holocene, and by about 7,000 years ago at the latest the strait was under water. After a fall from about 5,000 years ago, the islands at Adam's Bridge emerged again.

text.en: One source (Wikipedia). The article gives no dates of its own for Adam's Bridge. A study it cites tentatively concludes that there is not enough evidence that sea level has fallen, and explains raised reefs in southern India as probably caused by local uplift of the land. The span runs from the end of the ice age, which the article gives as 11,700 years ago, to 7,000 years ago; when the strait filled is not stated more precisely.

summary.en: Finds older than 42,000 years, among them fish bones, have been made in the limestone cave of Jerimalai on the eastern tip of Timor-Leste. The people there ate turtles, tuna and giant rats. According to the article, the fish bones are the oldest evidence of fishing far from the shore. A fish hook made of shell is thought to be 16,000–23,000 years old.

text.en: The article contradicts itself on the fish hooks: the introduction links hooks to the finds from 42,000 years ago, but the section on fishing says the hook is 16,000–23,000 years old. The statement about fishing far from the shore rests on news articles that the article cites. One source (Wikipedia).

summary.en: About 52,000 years ago a volcanic eruption formed a caldera on Sumatra, about 20 km long and 8 km wide. The eruption's deposits cover an estimated 8,500 km² and reached west as far as today's coast. Lake Maninjau, up to 165 metres deep, now lies in the caldera.

text.en: One source (Wikipedia). The age rests on a 2004 study of the eruption's deposits and is an estimate. The volume of the eruption is given as 220–250 km³, after a 1979 study.

summary.en: On Bali, Mount Batur has collapsed twice when the magma chamber collapsed. The first and larger caldera, 10 × 13 km, formed about 29,300 years ago, and an inner one about 20,150 years ago. The article’s source names carbon-14 dating in its title; whether the ages are calibrated is not stated.

text.en: Another estimate, linked to the Bali or Ubud ignimbrite, gives about 23,670 and 28,500 years ago for the inner caldera. The article does not say which estimate is more reliable. One source (Wikipedia).

summary.en: In Spirit Cave in northern Thailand, Chester Gorman found remains of about a dozen plant genera in the 1960s, among them betel nut and pepper, in layers from about 9800–8500 BC; the source does not say whether the years are calibrated. The finds were long seen as early farming, which has no support (Higham and Thosarat).

text.en: The article on Spirit Cave gives the layers in years BC and speaks in its introduction of uncalibrated radiocarbon years. The article on the Hoabinhian gives the same plant finds as 9,800–8,500 years before present, that is, about 1,950 years later. No plant differed from wild forms. Newer dates on crab claws (2021) give about 7850–6500 BC, and a date on resin (2003) about 1400 BC. Wilhelm Solheim pushed the farming interpretation furthest.

summary.en: At the coldest point of the ice age, the sea was about 120 metres lower than today, and the whole Sunda Shelf was land. Borneo, Java and Sumatra were then joined to the mainland. From about 18,000 years ago until about 5000 BC, large parts went under water, possibly in three large pulses of sea-level rise.

text.en: The article also says that large parts were dry from about 110,000 to 12,000 years ago, and does not explain how this fits with the flooding starting 18,000 years ago. The three pulses are given without dates. One source (Wikipedia), which cites Bellwood (2007).

summary.en: In 1913 a farmer in Antrea, then in Finland, found parts of a willow fishing net together with 31 net weights and 18 floats. The net is dated to about 8540 BC and sank into the clay at the bottom of the Ancylus Lake. It was about 27–30 metres long, with a mesh suited to salmon and bream.

text.en: The article on the net does not say how it was dated and calls it one of the oldest known fishing nets in the world. The article on Kamennogorsk instead describes nets of nettle fibre, up to 3 metres wide, while the article on the net says willow and 1.3–1.5 metres.

summary.en: The Salpausselkä is an end moraine that formed in front of the ice at the end of the ice age. According to one article, the water of Lake Saimaa broke through it about 5,000 years before present; another says the lake drained through a new outlet about 6,000 years ago. The outlet became the Vuoksi River, and the level of Ladoga rose by 1–2 metres.

text.en: The article on the Vuoksi does not say whether the years are radiocarbon or calendar years, nor where the breakthrough happened. The article on Lake Saimaa says the lake was suddenly drained through a new outlet about 6,000 years ago, but does not mention the Vuoksi. The information on the Salpausselkä rests on a popular science book from 1980. The article on the Salpausselkä describes only the ridge and does not mention the breakthrough. The span of 6,000–5,000 years ago shows that the figures differ.

summary.en: The Comb Ceramic culture existed from about 4200 to 2000 BC, from Finnmark in the north to the Vistula in the south. The finds suggest a fairly wide exchange: asbestos from Lake Saimaa, green slate from Lake Onega, amber from the southern Baltic coast and flint from the Valdai area. Flint arrowheads from Russia reached Kierikki in Finland.

text.en: The information comes from two Wikipedia articles, both lacking many citations. The article on Kierikki does not date the trade; Kierikki-type ceramics were used in 3500–3100 BC. Calibrated radiocarbon dates of comb ware give a wider span, 5600–2300 BC.

summary.en: Within today’s Nalchik lay one of the oldest known Eneolithic cemeteries in the North Caucasus, with 121 graves. Two of the dead have been dated to around 4900–4400 BC. The genome of a man buried there combines ancestry from hunter-gatherers of the Caucasus and Eastern Europe and from early farmers of West Asia.

text.en: A study in iScience (2024) dates the cemetery to around 5000/4800 BC; a study in Nature (2024) dates two of the dead to 4930–4686 and 4531–4359 BC. The cemetery was excavated in 1929, and only two of the graves have been preserved. The genome analysis rests on a single man, and the authors write that the context is not fully understood. The iScience authors describe it as the earliest collective Eneolithic burial ground in the North Caucasus. The same text gives two different dates for the Progress 2 burial (4994–4802 and 2476–2303 BC) without explaining the difference.

summary.en: A kurgan at Novokorsunskaya in the Kuban region held a wagon grave of the Maykop culture. The grave contained two solid wooden wheels, which Wikipedia dates to the second half of the fourth millennium BC (3500–3000 BC). The Maykop area has some of the oldest known wagon wheels in the world.

text.en: The information comes from two articles in English Wikipedia, on the Maykop culture and on chariot burials. They cite different books (Holm 2019; Baumer 2012 and Fowler et al. 2015), which we have not been able to open. Neither article says how the wheels were dated. Wikidata gives only the location of the village.

summary.en: Near Maikop in the North Caucasus stood a burial mound about ten metres high. Nikolay Veselovsky excavated it in 1897. The main grave was rich and held, among other things, bull figurines of gold and silver, and the mound also contained two women’s graves. The finds are in the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg.

text.en: The dates do not come from a dating of the grave itself. Wikipedia quotes the archaeologist David Anthony (2010) as saying that the grave was contemporary with the Uruk period in Mesopotamia, 3700–3100 BC. According to the article on the Maykop culture, radiocarbon dates of the culture’s sites are given as 3950, 3650, 3610 and 2980 BC, that is from 3950 to 2980 BC. Wikidata gives the point.

summary.en: At the Sagan-Zaba II site on Lake Baikal, people were hunting Baikal seals at least 9,000 years ago. Sealing peaked about 6,700–4,900 years ago, when 94–98 per cent of the identified animal bones in those layers were seal. Most of the seals were taken in spring. Later, fish and hoofed animals became more important.

text.en: Dates and text come only from one study (PLoS One 2015). Seal bones give ages that are too old, because the lake contains old carbon (about 700 years), so the layers were dated with bones of hoofed animals. The study gives no coordinates. The point is the village of Buguldeyka according to Wikidata; according to the study, the Bugul’deika II site lies about 40 km southwest of Sagan-Zaba. The start and end years here correspond to layer VII (9020–8650 calibrated years before 1950), when sealing begins; across the whole find, 82.8 per cent of the identified bones were seal; the peak comes later and lasts longer, about 6750–4870 years before 1950.

summary.en: During the Ice Age a land bridge joined Asia and North America. When the ice melted the sea rose. According to sediment cores, the Bering Strait was flooded about 11,500 years ago, linking the Pacific and Arctic Oceans. The spread of species suggests a shallow connection already about 13,300 years ago.

text.en: Sediment cores give dates between about 10,900 and 12,000 years ago, together about 11,000–11,500 years ago, and the spread of species about 13,300 years ago. The study in Science Advances (2020) reconciles them with a period when the sea fell or stood still. Wikipedia gives about 11,000 years ago and in another place about 10,000 years ago. That water through the strait contributed to the cold Younger Dryas period is the study’s hypothesis.

summary.en: On Zhokhov Island, far north of Siberia, tools, a possible sledge runner and dog bones have been found. The inhabitants hunted polar bears and reindeer. A dog’s jaw has a calibrated age of about 9,500 years, and the dog belongs to a lineage related to today’s sled dogs. The finds have been seen as a possible early sign of dog breeding.

text.en: Wikipedia states, citing Pitulʹko (1993), that people were on the island as early as about 6000 BC. The dog’s jaw has a calibrated age of 9,524 years before present (Science 2020), that is about 7600 BC; the study does not say which material was dated, and it calls the sledge remains putative. That study is not openly licensed and is used only for the date. That the remains come from sledges is an interpretation, and the claim about breeding rests on a news article in Science in 2017 that Wikipedia cites.

summary.en: Ksudach is a stratovolcano in southern Kamchatka with several calderas nested inside one another. The volcano has collapsed five times, three of them after the Ice Age. Eruptions have been radiocarbon-dated to 8,700–8,800 and 6,000–6,100 years before present. A large eruption around AD 240 formed the fifth and most recent caldera.

text.en: One source (Wikipedia). Wikipedia gives the ages as radiocarbon years before present without saying whether they are calibrated, so the calendar years may differ. The start and end years here are counted from 1950 (8,800 and 6,000 years before present). The article does not say which caldera formed in which of the eruptions before AD 240. The span covers two eruptive phases with a gap between them, not one long eruption.
